statement_analysis.statement: The National Judicial Appointments Commission comprised the Chief Justice of India, two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons — one of whom was to be nominated by the Chief Justice alone.
statement_analysis.reason: The two eminent persons under the NJAC were to be selected by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India, and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha — not by the CJI alone.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment in 2016, holding it unconstitutional on grounds of violating the basic structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The NJAC judgment was delivered in 2015, not 2016. The five-judge bench struck it down by a 4:1 majority in October 2015.

statement_analysis.statement: The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted new Articles 124A, 124B, and 124C into the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The 99th Amendment did insert Articles 124A (NJAC establishment), 124B (functions), and 124C (power to make regulations), making Statement 3 factually accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (3 only) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 3 as accurate may assume it is the only incorrect one, not realising the question asks for statements that are NOT correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 misattributes eminent-person selection to CJI alone — NOT correct.
Statement 2 incorrectly states 2016; the verdict was in 2015 — NOT correct.
Statement 3 is factually accurate and therefore not an answer to 'which are NOT correct'.
Select option (a): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate simultaneously here. First, the NJAC year is commonly misremembered as 2016 rather than 2015. Second, the eminent-person selection mechanism is frequently recalled incorrectly — students remember 'CJI is involved' but forget the PM and LoP are equal partners in that selection. Statement 3 is included as a factually correct statement to prevent mechanical elimination.
solution.final_explanation:
The NJAC was constituted under the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014, which inserted Articles 124A, 124B, and 124C. The Supreme Court's Constitution Bench (4:1 majority) struck it down in October 2015 as violating judicial independence — a basic structure element.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The two eminent persons were selected by a three-member committee (PM + CJI + Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha), not by the CJI unilaterally. This is a key structural detail.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The judgment was delivered in 2015, not 2016. Justice Chelameswar dissented; the other four judges held it unconstitutional.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 99th Amendment did insert Articles 124A, 124B, and 124C. It also amended Articles 127, 128, 217, 222, 224, 224A, and 231.

Value Addition:
• Justice Chelameswar's lone dissent argued NJAC was constitutionally valid — important for essay/mains.
• The NJAC case is also called the Fourth Judges Case.
• Post-NJAC verdict, a revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) is still being negotiated.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Judicial Appointments Commission comprised the Chief Justice of India, two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons — one of whom was to be nominated by the Chief Justice alone.
statement_analysis.reason: NJAC के तहत दो प्रमुख व्यक्तियों का चयन प्रधानमंत्री, भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश और लोकसभा में विपक्ष के नेता की समिति द्वारा किया जाना था — न कि केवल CJI द्वारा।

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment in 2016, holding it unconstitutional on grounds of violating the basic structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: NJAC का निर्णय 2016 में नहीं, बल्कि 2015 में दिया गया था। पांच न्यायाधीशों की पीठ ने अक्टूबर 2015 में 4:1 बहुमत से इसे खारिज किया था।

statement_analysis.statement: The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted new Articles 124A, 124B, and 124C into the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: 99वें संशोधन ने वास्तव में संविधान में अनुच्छेद 124A (NJAC की स्थापना), 124B (कार्य), और 124C (नियम बनाने का अधिकार) जोड़े, इसलिए कथन 3 तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है।

solution.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प c (केवल 3) एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला है क्योंकि जो छात्र कथन 3 को सही पहचानते हैं वे मान सकते हैं कि यह एकमात्र गलत कथन है, जबकि प्रश्न उन कथनों के लिए है जो सही नहीं हैं।
elimination_logic: कथन 1 में प्रमुख व्यक्तियों के चयन को केवल CJI से जोड़ना सही नहीं है।
कथन 2 में वर्ष 2016 गलत है; निर्णय 2015 में दिया गया था।
कथन 3 तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है, अतः यह 'सही नहीं है' वाले प्रश्न का उत्तर नहीं हो सकता।
अतः विकल्प (a) चुनें: केवल 1 और 2।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: यहाँ दो जाल एक साथ काम करते हैं। पहला, NJAC का वर्ष अक्सर 2016 के बजाय 2015 के रूप में गलत याद किया जाता है। दूसरा, प्रमुख व्यक्तियों के चयन की प्रक्रिया अक्सर गलत याद की जाती है — छात्र याद करते हैं कि 'CJI शामिल है' लेकिन भूल जाते हैं कि PM और विपक्ष के नेता भी समान भागीदार हैं। कथन 3 को तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही शामिल किया गया है ताकि यांत्रिक रूप से उसे बाहर न किया जाए।
solution.final_explanation:
NJAC की स्थापना 99वें संविधान संशोधन अधिनियम, 2014 के तहत हुई थी, जिसने अनुच्छेद 124A, 124B, और 124C जोड़े। सुप्रीम कोर्ट की संविधान पीठ (4:1 बहुमत) ने अक्टूबर 2015 में इसे न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता के उल्लंघन के कारण खारिज कर दिया — जो मूल संरचना का हिस्सा है।

• कथन 1 — सही नहीं है: दो प्रमुख व्यक्तियों का चयन तीन सदस्यीय समिति (PM + CJI + लोकसभा में विपक्ष के नेता) द्वारा किया जाता था, न कि CJI अकेले। यह एक महत्वपूर्ण संरचनात्मक विवरण है।
• कथन 2 — सही नहीं है: निर्णय 2015 में दिया गया था, 2016 में नहीं। न्यायाधीश चेलमेश्वर ने असहमतिपूर्ण मत दिया; अन्य चार न्यायाधीशों ने इसे असंवैधानिक माना।
• कथन 3 — सही है: 99वें संशोधन ने अनुच्छेद 124A, 124B, और 124C जोड़े। साथ ही अनुच्छेद 127, 128, 217, 222, 224, 224A, और 231 में भी संशोधन किया।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• न्यायाधीश चेलमेश्वर का एकल असहमतिपूर्ण मत था कि NJAC संवैधानिक रूप से वैध था — निबंध/मुख्य परीक्षा के लिए महत्वपूर्ण।
• NJAC मामला चौथा न्यायाधीश मामला भी कहलाता है।
• NJAC निर्णय के बाद, संशोधित प्रक्रिया ज्ञापन (MoP) अभी भी बातचीत के अधीन है।

solution.concept_anchor: Consultees for SC vs HC judge appointments

statement_analysis.statement: Governor of the concerned state is consulted for appointment of a High Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(1) explicitly requires the President to consult the Governor of the state while appointing HC judges — this is mandatory.

statement_analysis.statement: Governor of the concerned state is consulted for appointment of a Supreme Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(2) requires consultation with the CJI (and other SC judges and HC judges as deemed necessary) but does NOT include the Governor for SC appointments.

statement_analysis.statement: Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is consulted for appointment of a High Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(1) mandates consultation with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court in addition to CJI and Governor.

statement_analysis.statement: Chief Justice of India is consulted for both Supreme Court and High Court judge appointments.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(2) mandates CJI consultation for SC appointments; Article 217(1) mandates CJI consultation for HC appointments as well.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is a strong distractor because students who correctly eliminate Statement 2 may miscalculate the remaining correct statements or confuse the HC consultee list.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correct — Governor IS consulted for HC under Article 217(1).
Statement 2 incorrect — Governor is NOT consulted for SC appointments under Article 124(2).
Statements 3 and 4 are both correct.
Three correct pairs — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Governor's role is the key trap here. Students correctly remember that Governor is involved in HC appointments and mistakenly extend that to SC appointments. Article 124(2) has no mention of the Governor — this is one of the most commonly confused procedural distinctions in judicial appointment questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The consultative process differs significantly between SC and HC appointments, and Statement 2 is the trap planted here.

| Pair | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Governor consulted for HC judge | Correct — Article 217(1) |
| Governor consulted for SC judge | Incorrect — Article 124(2) |
| HC Chief Justice consulted for HC judge | Correct — Article 217(1) |
| CJI consulted for both SC and HC | Correct — Articles 124(2) and 217(1) |

Three of the four pairs are correctly stated.

Value Addition:
• For HC appointments: Three mandatory consultees — CJI, Governor of state, and Chief Justice of that HC.
• For SC appointments: Mandatory consultee is CJI; other judges consulted as President deems necessary.
• Post-Second Judges Case (1993), 'consultation' with CJI became 'concurrence' in practice.

statement_analysis.statement: संबंधित राज्य के राज्यपाल से उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की नियुक्ति के लिए परामर्श किया जाता है।
statement_analysis.reason: अनुच्छेद 217(1) स्पष्ट रूप से राष्ट्रपति को उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों की नियुक्ति करते समय संबंधित राज्य के राज्यपाल से परामर्श करना अनिवार्य करता है।

statement_analysis.statement: संबंधित राज्य के राज्यपाल से सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की नियुक्ति के लिए परामर्श किया जाता है।
statement_analysis.reason: अनुच्छेद 124(2) में मुख्य न्यायाधीश (CJI) और आवश्यकतानुसार अन्य सर्वोच्च न्यायालय तथा उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों से परामर्श करने का प्रावधान है, लेकिन इसमें सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए राज्यपाल का उल्लेख नहीं है।

statement_analysis.statement: संबंधित उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश से उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की नियुक्ति के लिए परामर्श किया जाता है।
statement_analysis.reason: अनुच्छेद 217(1) में मुख्य न्यायाधीश और राज्यपाल के साथ-साथ संबंधित उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश से परामर्श करना अनिवार्य है।

statement_analysis.statement: भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश से दोनों सर्वोच्च न्यायालय और उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों की नियुक्ति के लिए परामर्श किया जाता है।
statement_analysis.reason: अनुच्छेद 124(2) में सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए CJI से परामर्श अनिवार्य है; अनुच्छेद 217(1) में उच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए भी CJI से परामर्श अनिवार्य है।

solution.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प c (केवल तीन) एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला विकल्प है क्योंकि जो छात्र कथन 2 को सही ढंग से खारिज कर देते हैं, वे शेष सही कथनों की संख्या गलत समझ सकते हैं या उच्च न्यायालय के परामर्श सूची को भ्रमित कर सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: कथन 1 सही है — अनुच्छेद 217(1) के तहत राज्यपाल से उच्च न्यायालय के लिए परामर्श किया जाता है।
कथन 2 गलत है — अनुच्छेद 124(2) के तहत सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए राज्यपाल से परामर्श नहीं किया जाता।
कथन 3 और 4 दोनों सही हैं।
तीन सही जोड़े हैं — विकल्प (c) चुनें: केवल तीन।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: यहाँ राज्यपाल की भूमिका मुख्य जाल है। छात्र सही रूप से याद रखते हैं कि राज्यपाल उच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों में शामिल होता है और गलती से इसे सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों तक बढ़ा देते हैं। अनुच्छेद 124(2) में राज्यपाल का कोई उल्लेख नहीं है — यह न्यायिक नियुक्ति प्रश्नों में सबसे सामान्य भ्रमित करने वाले प्रक्रियात्मक भेदों में से एक है।
solution.final_explanation:
सर्वोच्च न्यायालय और उच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए परामर्श प्रक्रिया में महत्वपूर्ण अंतर है, और कथन 2 यहाँ जाल है।

| जोड़ा | निर्णय |
|---|---|
| उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश के लिए राज्यपाल से परामर्श | सही — अनुच्छेद 217(1) |
| सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश के लिए राज्यपाल से परामर्श | गलत — अनुच्छेद 124(2) |
| उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश के लिए उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश से परामर्श | सही — अनुच्छेद 217(1) |
| दोनों सर्वोच्च न्यायालय और उच्च न्यायालय के लिए CJI से परामर्श | सही — अनुच्छेद 124(2) और 217(1) |

चार में से तीन जोड़े सही बताए गए हैं।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• उच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए तीन अनिवार्य परामर्शकर्ता — CJI, राज्य के राज्यपाल, और संबंधित उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश।
• सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्तियों के लिए अनिवार्य परामर्शकर्ता CJI है; अन्य न्यायाधीशों से राष्ट्रपति आवश्यकतानुसार परामर्श करता है।
• द्वितीय न्यायाधीश मामला (1993) के बाद, CJI के साथ 'परामर्श' व्यवहार में 'सहमति' बन गया।

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly places Article 127 with ad hoc judges but swaps the descriptions of Articles 126 and 128, exploiting the common confusion between 'acting' and 'requested' retired judges.
elimination_logic: Article 126 = acting CJI (President's appointment, no consultation) — matches description 3.
Article 127 = ad hoc judges who are sitting HC judges — matches description 1.
Article 128 = retired SC judges 'requested' by CJI — matches description 2.
Select option (c): A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The critical trap is the distinction between Article 127 (ad hoc judges = sitting HC judges) and Article 128 (retired SC judges who are 'requested', not 'appointed'). Students frequently conflate these two provisions or assume both deal with retired judges. The word 'requested' in Article 128 versus 'appointed' in Article 127 is a nuance UPSC has tested indirectly.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 126, 127, 128, and 224A each address a distinct category of non-regular judicial appointment. Getting the match right requires distinguishing among these precisely.

Correct pairings:
• A (Article 126) — 3: President appoints acting CJI when office is vacant or CJI cannot perform duties; no consultation is mandated.
• B (Article 127) — 1: President appoints ad hoc SC judges, who are sitting HC judges, with consent of CJI and the concerned HC Chief Justice.
• C (Article 128) — 2: CJI may 'request' (not appoint) retired SC judges to sit with President's prior consent — they are not formally appointed.
• D (Article 224A) — 4: HC Chief Justice may request retired HC judges to sit, requiring consent of the retired judge and the President.

Common trap pairings: Articles 127 and 128 are often swapped because both involve temporary SC sittings, but Article 127 uses sitting HC judges while Article 128 uses retired SC judges.

Value Addition:
• Under Article 128, retired judges are 'requested' — they retain the right to decline.
• Article 224A requires the retired HC judge's own consent, unlike Article 127.
• Acting CJI under Article 126 is a President's prerogative with no mandatory consultation.

solution.concept_anchor: अनुच्छेद 126, 127, 128 — कार्यवाहक और अस्थायी सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश
solution.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प b एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला है क्योंकि यह सही ढंग से अनुच्छेद 127 को अस्थायी न्यायाधीशों के साथ रखता है लेकिन अनुच्छेद 126 और 128 के विवरणों को बदल देता है, जो 'कार्यवाहक' और 'अनुरोधित' सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीशों के बीच आम भ्रम का लाभ उठाता है।
elimination_logic: अनुच्छेद 126 = कार्यवाहक मुख्य न्यायाधीश (राष्ट्रपति की नियुक्ति, कोई परामर्श आवश्यक नहीं) — विवरण 3 से मेल खाता है।
अनुच्छेद 127 = अस्थायी न्यायाधीश जो वर्तमान में उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश हैं — विवरण 1 से मेल खाता है।
अनुच्छेद 128 = सेवानिवृत्त सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश जिन्हें मुख्य न्यायाधीश द्वारा 'अनुरोधित' किया जाता है — विवरण 2 से मेल खाता है।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: महत्वपूर्ण जाल अनुच्छेद 127 (अस्थायी न्यायाधीश = वर्तमान उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश) और अनुच्छेद 128 (सेवानिवृत्त सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश जिन्हें 'अनुरोधित' किया जाता है, न कि 'नियुक्त') के बीच का अंतर है। छात्र अक्सर इन दोनों प्रावधानों को मिलाते हैं या मान लेते हैं कि दोनों सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीशों से संबंधित हैं। अनुच्छेद 128 में 'अनुरोधित' शब्द और अनुच्छेद 127 में 'नियुक्त' शब्द के बीच का सूक्ष्म अंतर UPSC ने अप्रत्यक्ष रूप से परखा है।
solution.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 126, 127, 128, और 224A प्रत्येक गैर-नियमित न्यायिक नियुक्ति की एक विशिष्ट श्रेणी को संबोधित करते हैं। सही मेल पाने के लिए इन्हें सटीक रूप से अलग करना आवश्यक है।

सही जोड़े:
• A (अनुच्छेद 126) — 3: जब पद रिक्त हो या मुख्य न्यायाधीश कर्तव्य नहीं निभा सकते, तो राष्ट्रपति कार्यवाहक मुख्य न्यायाधीश नियुक्त करता है; कोई परामर्श अनिवार्य नहीं है।
• B (अनुच्छेद 127) — 1: राष्ट्रपति अस्थायी सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश नियुक्त करता है, जो वर्तमान में उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश होते हैं, मुख्य न्यायाधीश और संबंधित उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश की सहमति से।
• C (अनुच्छेद 128) — 2: मुख्य न्यायाधीश सेवानिवृत्त सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों से राष्ट्रपति की पूर्व सहमति से 'अनुरोध' कर सकते हैं — ये औपचारिक रूप से नियुक्त नहीं होते।
• D (अनुच्छेद 224A) — 4: उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश सेवानिवृत्त उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों से अनुरोध कर सकते हैं, जिसके लिए सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीश और राष्ट्रपति की सहमति आवश्यक है।

सामान्य भ्रम के जोड़े: अनुच्छेद 127 और 128 को अक्सर उलट दिया जाता है क्योंकि दोनों अस्थायी सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की बैठकों से संबंधित हैं, लेकिन अनुच्छेद 127 वर्तमान उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों का उपयोग करता है जबकि अनुच्छेद 128 सेवानिवृत्त सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों का।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• अनुच्छेद 128 के तहत, सेवानिवृत्त न्यायाधीशों से 'अनुरोध' किया जाता है — वे अस्वीकार करने का अधिकार रखते हैं।
• अनुच्छेद 224A में सेवानिवृत्त उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की अपनी सहमति आवश्यक है, जो अनुच्छेद 127 से भिन्न है।
• अनुच्छेद 126 के तहत कार्यवाहक मुख्य न्यायाधीश राष्ट्रपति की विशेषाधिकार है जिसमें कोई अनिवार्य परामर्श नहीं होता।

Special Majority Requirement for Impeachment — Constitutional Nuances

solution.concept_anchor: Impeachment special majority — absolute plus qualified threshold
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students who do not carefully examine the causal link will assume R explains A.
elimination_logic: A is correct — Article 124(4) mandates both absolute and 2/3 qualified majority simultaneously.
R is correct — no SC judge has ever been successfully impeached.
R does not causally explain A — zero removals is a historical outcome, not the reason for the high threshold.
Select option (b): Both correct, R is not the explanation of A.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap operates through reversed causation. The high impeachment threshold (A) is a deliberate constitutional design to protect judicial independence. The fact that no judge has ever been removed (R) is an empirical outcome partly attributable to that threshold — making R a consequence of A, not its explanation. Students who see two true statements instinctively mark option (a), missing the causal direction test.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 124(4) prescribes a uniquely demanding removal process for SC judges, combining two separate majority requirements that must be satisfied simultaneously.

Assertion Analysis: The removal address requires (i) majority of total membership of the House (absolute majority) AND (ii) two-thirds of members present and voting (qualified majority). Both must be met in each House in the same session — making this harder than an ordinary special majority that requires only the qualified component.

Reason Analysis: Factually accurate — no SC judge has ever been successfully impeached. Justice V. Ramaswami's motion in 1993 passed the Rajya Sabha but failed in the Lok Sabha when the Congress party abstained. Justice Dipak Misra's notice in 2018 was rejected by the Rajya Sabha Chairman.

Causal Relationship: R does not explain A. The high threshold is a constitutional design choice rooted in the need for judicial independence — it existed from the Constitution's commencement. The fact of zero successful removals is a historical outcome, possibly influenced by A, but not its explanatory cause.

Value Addition:
• Same dual-majority requirement applies to removal of the CAG and (post-2023) Election Commissioners.
• Both Houses must pass the address in the same session.
• Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 governs the three-member investigative committee that precedes any address.

Special Majority Requirement for Impeachment — Constitutional Nuances

solution.concept_anchor: Impeachment special majority — absolute plus qualified threshold
solution.strong_distractor: a — विकल्प a एक मजबूत भ्रमकारी है क्योंकि दोनों A और R तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही हैं, और जो छात्र कारणात्मक संबंध को सावधानीपूर्वक नहीं देखते वे मान लेते हैं कि R, A की व्याख्या करता है।
elimination_logic: A सही है — अनुच्छेद 124(4) एक साथ पूर्ण बहुमत और 2/3 योग्य बहुमत दोनों की आवश्यकता करता है।
R सही है — अब तक कोई भी सुप्रीम कोर्ट न्यायाधीश सफलतापूर्वक महाभियोग के माध्यम से हटाया नहीं गया है।
R, A की कारणात्मक व्याख्या नहीं करता — शून्य हटाने का तथ्य एक ऐतिहासिक परिणाम है, उच्च सीमा का कारण नहीं।
विकल्प (b) चुनें: दोनों सही हैं, लेकिन R, A की व्याख्या नहीं है।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: यह जाल उल्टे कारण-प्रभाव के माध्यम से काम करता है। उच्च महाभियोग सीमा (A) न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता की रक्षा के लिए संवैधानिक रूप से डिज़ाइन की गई है। यह तथ्य कि कोई न्यायाधीश कभी हटाया नहीं गया (R), आंशिक रूप से उस सीमा के कारण है — अतः R, A का परिणाम है, व्याख्या नहीं। जो छात्र दो सत्य कथन देखते हैं वे स्वाभाविक रूप से विकल्प (a) चुन लेते हैं, लेकिन कारणात्मक दिशा की परीक्षा से चूक जाते हैं।
solution.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 124(4) सुप्रीम कोर्ट न्यायाधीशों के हटाने की एक विशिष्ट और कठिन प्रक्रिया निर्धारित करता है, जिसमें दो अलग-अलग बहुमत आवश्यकताएँ एक साथ पूरी करनी होती हैं।

कथन विश्लेषण: हटाने के प्रस्ताव के लिए (i) सदन की कुल सदस्यता का बहुमत (पूर्ण बहुमत) और (ii) उपस्थित और मतदान करने वाले सदस्यों का दो-तिहाई बहुमत (योग्य बहुमत) आवश्यक है। दोनों सदनों में एक ही सत्र में यह दोनों शर्तें पूरी करनी होती हैं — जो सामान्य विशेष बहुमत से कठिन है जिसमें केवल योग्य बहुमत की आवश्यकता होती है।

कारण विश्लेषण: तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही — भारत में कोई भी सुप्रीम कोर्ट न्यायाधीश सफलतापूर्वक महाभियोग के माध्यम से हटाया नहीं गया है। न्यायमूर्ति वी. रामास्वामी का 1993 में प्रस्ताव राज्यसभा में पारित हुआ लेकिन लोकसभा में कांग्रेस पार्टी के बहिष्कार के कारण असफल रहा। न्यायमूर्ति दीपक मिश्रा का 2018 का नोटिस राज्यसभा अध्यक्ष द्वारा खारिज कर दिया गया।

कारणात्मक संबंध: R, A की व्याख्या नहीं करता। उच्च सीमा न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता की आवश्यकता से उत्पन्न संवैधानिक डिज़ाइन है — यह संविधान के प्रारंभ से ही मौजूद है। शून्य सफल हटाने का तथ्य एक ऐतिहासिक परिणाम है, संभवतः A से प्रभावित, लेकिन इसका कारण नहीं।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• समान दोहरी बहुमत की आवश्यकता CAG और (2023 के बाद) चुनाव आयुक्तों के हटाने पर भी लागू होती है।
• दोनों सदनों को एक ही सत्र में प्रस्ताव पारित करना होता है।

solution.final_explanation:
Four landmark events shaped the evolution of CJI appointments from political controversy to the near-binding seniority convention of today.

Correct sequence:
1. 1973 — Justice A.N. Ray appointed CJI superseding three senior judges (J.M. Shelat, K.S. Hegde, A.N. Grover), a politically controversial move during Indira Gandhi's government.
2. 1977 — Justice M.H. Beg appointed CJI superseding Justice H.R. Khanna, who had dissented in the ADM Jabalpur habeas corpus case.
3. 1993 — Second Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record) established judicial primacy, treating CJI's collegium opinion as binding.
4. 2015 — NJAC judgment (Fourth Judges Case) struck down the 99th Amendment, cementing the collegium.

Wrong options fail by reversing the two supersessions or misplacing the Judges Cases relative to the NJAC judgment.

• Justice H.R. Khanna's supersession in 1977 is regarded as one of the darkest episodes in Indian judicial history.
• Post-1993, seniority convention for CJI has not been violated.
• The Constitution (Article 124(2)) is silent on seniority for CJI — convention fills the gap.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 222 — HC judge transfer without consent
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students assume that a constitutional functionary's transfer requires the consent of affected parties, drawing an incorrect analogy with IAS transfers under state government.
elimination_logic: Article 222 does not require the judge's consent — eliminate options premised on that.
Governor is a consultee for HC appointments (Article 217), not transfers — eliminate option (b).
Post-1993, CJI collegium's concurrence is the binding safeguard for transfers — option (c) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The consent requirement is the trap. Students analogise judicial transfers to civil service transfers where affected officers may have recourse, or to appointment processes where multiple consultees must agree. Article 222 requires only Presidential action after consulting the CJI — the judge being transferred has no constitutional veto, and the Governor of either state is not a required consultee.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 222 empowers the President to transfer a judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India. Post-Second Judges Case (1993), this consultation has hardened into a requirement of the CJI collegium's concurrence.

Applicable principle: The transferred judge's personal consent is NOT constitutionally required. The Governor of the state is NOT a required consultee for transfers (unlike appointments under Article 217). The S.P. Gupta case (1981) had upheld the validity of such transfers; post-1993, the CJI's binding concurrence serves as the judicial check.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No constitutional provision requires the judge's consent before transfer under Article 222.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Governor's concurrence is required for HC judge appointments (Article 217), not transfers — a classic conflation.
• Option (c) — Correct: The transfer is constitutionally valid. The CJI collegium's concurrence is the operative safeguard, not judicial or gubernatorial consent.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The transfer cannot be voided merely because the judge did not consent — the judge has no constitutional veto over transfers.

Value Addition:
• Chief Justice of a HC can also be transferred under Article 222.
• Post-1993, the collegium's role in transfers is equivalent to its role in appointments.
• Transfer is not a punitive measure constitutionally — though concerns about its misuse persist.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: सहमति की आवश्यकता एक जाल है। छात्र न्यायिक स्थानांतरणों की तुलना सिविल सेवा स्थानांतरणों से करते हैं जहाँ प्रभावित अधिकारी पुनर्विचार कर सकते हैं, या नियुक्ति प्रक्रियाओं से जहाँ कई सलाहकारों की सहमति आवश्यक होती है। अनुच्छेद 222 केवल राष्ट्रपति की कार्रवाई की मांग करता है जो CJI से परामर्श के बाद होती है — स्थानांतरित न्यायाधीश का कोई संवैधानिक वीटो नहीं है, और किसी भी राज्य के राज्यपाल की सहमति आवश्यक सलाहकार नहीं है।
solution.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 222 राष्ट्रपति को एक उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश को दूसरे उच्च न्यायालय में स्थानांतरित करने का अधिकार देता है, बशर्ते वह भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश से परामर्श करे। दूसरे जज केस (1993) के बाद, यह परामर्श CJI कॉलेजियम की सहमति के रूप में कठोर हो गया है।

लागू सिद्धांत: स्थानांतरित न्यायाधीश की व्यक्तिगत सहमति संवैधानिक रूप से आवश्यक नहीं है। स्थानांतरण के लिए राज्यपाल आवश्यक सलाहकार नहीं हैं (जैसे कि नियुक्तियों के लिए अनुच्छेद 217 के तहत)। S.P. Gupta केस (1981) ने ऐसे स्थानांतरणों की वैधता को स्वीकार किया था; 1993 के बाद, CJI की बाध्यकारी सहमति न्यायिक जांच के रूप में कार्य करती है।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: अनुच्छेद 222 के तहत स्थानांतरण से पहले न्यायाधीश की सहमति की कोई संवैधानिक आवश्यकता नहीं है।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: राज्यपाल की सहमति HC न्यायाधीश की नियुक्ति (अनुच्छेद 217) के लिए आवश्यक है, स्थानांतरण के लिए नहीं — यह एक सामान्य भ्रम है।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: स्थानांतरण संवैधानिक रूप से वैध है। CJI कॉलेजियम की सहमति कार्यकारी सुरक्षा है, न कि न्यायिक या राज्यपाल की सहमति।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: केवल इसलिए कि न्यायाधीश की सहमति नहीं मिली, स्थानांतरण को रद्द नहीं किया जा सकता — न्यायाधीश के पास स्थानांतरण पर कोई संवैधानिक वीटो नहीं है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• एक उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश को भी अनुच्छेद 222 के तहत स्थानांतरित किया जा सकता है।
• 1993 के बाद, स्थानांतरण में कॉलेजियम की भूमिका नियुक्ति में उसकी भूमिका के बराबर है।
• स्थानांतरण संवैधानिक रूप से दंडात्मक उपाय नहीं है — हालांकि इसके दुरुपयोग की चिंताएँ बनी हुई हैं।

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap operates between the Vice President's removal and judicial impeachment. Both involve Parliament, and students who remember 'Parliament removes these officials' group them together. The Vice President's removal under Article 67(b) requires only a majority in the Rajya Sabha (after 14 days' notice), agreed to by the Lok Sabha — no special majority, no synchronous session requirement. This is fundamentally different from the judicial impeachment process.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the precise removal mechanisms for different constitutional functionaries. SC judges, HC judges, and the Comptroller and Auditor General all share the same parliamentary address mechanism under Articles 124(4) and 218.

• Option (a) — Judge of the Supreme Court: Removed by address with absolute majority + 2/3 qualified majority in each House in the same session — the standard.
• Option (b) — Vice President: Removed under Article 67(b) by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. No special majority, no same-session requirement — this is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Comptroller and Auditor General: Article 148(1) explicitly applies the same process as Article 124(4) — identical to SC judge removal.
• Option (d) — Judge of a High Court: Article 218 makes Articles 124(4) and 124(5) applicable to HC judges — identical process.

Value Addition:
• President is impeached under Article 61 — by special majority in either House, then the other House investigates.
• Election Commissioners (post-2023 amendment) removed by same process as SC judges.
• Governors are not removed by Parliament — they hold office at President's pleasure.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: भ्रमित करने वाला जाल उपराष्ट्रपति की हटाने की प्रक्रिया और न्यायिक महाभियोग के बीच काम करता है। दोनों में संसद शामिल है, और छात्र जो याद करते हैं कि 'संसद इन अधिकारियों को हटाती है' उन्हें एक साथ जोड़ देते हैं। अनुच्छेद 67(ख) के तहत उपराष्ट्रपति को हटाने के लिए केवल राज्यसभा में बहुमत (14 दिन की सूचना के बाद) आवश्यक है, जिसे लोकसभा द्वारा सहमति दी जाती है — कोई विशेष बहुमत या एक ही सत्र की आवश्यकता नहीं। यह न्यायिक महाभियोग प्रक्रिया से मौलिक रूप से भिन्न है।
solution.final_explanation:
यह प्रश्न विभिन्न संवैधानिक पदाधिकारियों के हटाने के सटीक तंत्रों का परीक्षण करता है। सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीश, उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश, और नियंत्रक एवं महालेखा परीक्षक सभी अनुच्छेद 124(4) और 218 के तहत समान संसदीय संबोधन तंत्र साझा करते हैं।

• विकल्प (a) — सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीश: पूर्ण बहुमत + प्रत्येक सदन में उपस्थित और मतदान करने वाले सदस्यों के 2/3 बहुमत से उसी सत्र में संबोधन द्वारा हटाए जाते हैं — मानक प्रक्रिया।
• विकल्प (b) — उपराष्ट्रपति: अनुच्छेद 67(ख) के तहत राज्यसभा के बहुमत से पारित प्रस्ताव द्वारा और लोकसभा की सहमति से हटाए जाते हैं। कोई विशेष बहुमत या एक ही सत्र की आवश्यकता नहीं — यह अलग विकल्प है।
• विकल्प (c) — नियंत्रक एवं महालेखा परीक्षक: अनुच्छेद 148(1) स्पष्ट रूप से अनुच्छेद 124(4) की समान प्रक्रिया लागू करता है — सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीश के हटाने के समान।
• विकल्प (d) — उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश: अनुच्छेद 218 उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों पर अनुच्छेद 124(4) और 124(5) लागू करता है — समान प्रक्रिया।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• राष्ट्रपति को अनुच्छेद 61 के तहत महाभियोग के द्वारा हटाया जाता है — किसी भी सदन में विशेष बहुमत से, फिर दूसरे सदन द्वारा जांच।
• चुनाव आयुक्तों (2023 के संशोधन के बाद) को सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों के समान प्रक्रिया से हटाया जाता है।
• राज्यपालों को संसद द्वारा नहीं हटाया जाता — वे राष्ट्रपति की इच्छा पर पद पर रहते हैं।

solution.concept_anchor: SC vs HC judge retirement age and post-retirement practice restrictions

statement_analysis.statement: Judges of the Supreme Court of India retire at the age of sixty-five years, while judges of High Courts retire at the age of sixty-two years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(2) for SC and Article 217(1) for HC specify these retirement ages — 65 for SC and 62 for HC judges.

statement_analysis.statement: After retirement, a Supreme Court judge is prohibited from practising in any court or before any authority in India, whereas a retired High Court judge is prohibited only from practising before the High Court in which he or she served.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(7) bars retired SC judges from practising in any court or authority in India. Article 220 bars retired HC judges only from practising before the HC where they were a permanent judge — they may appear in other HCs or the SC.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know the retirement ages correctly may assume the post-retirement restriction for HC judges is more expansive than it actually is, making Statement 2 seem incorrect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correct — 65 years for SC (Article 124) and 62 years for HC (Article 217).
Statement 2 correct — SC bar is absolute (Article 124(7)); HC bar is limited to that specific HC (Article 220).
Both statements correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The post-retirement restriction asymmetry is the trap. Students tend to assume that the restriction for HC judges mirrors the SC restriction and extends to all courts. Article 220 is narrowly worded — it bars the specific HC where the judge was a permanent judge, not all courts. This creates a scenario where a retired HC judge can appear before the Supreme Court, which many students find counterintuitive.
solution.final_explanation:
Two distinct constitutional provisions govern the service conditions and post-retirement restrictions of SC and HC judges.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SC judges retire at 65 (Article 124(2)); HC judges at 62 (Article 217(1)). This three-year gap is a standard UPSC test point.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 124(7) applies a total bar on post-retirement practice for SC judges — they cannot appear before any court or authority in India. Article 220, however, bars a retired HC judge only from the specific HC where he or she served as a permanent judge. A retired HC judge can appear before the SC or other HCs.

Value Addition:
• Salaries of SC judges are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India; HC judges' salaries to Consolidated Fund of the respective State.
• Parliament can change service conditions prospectively but cannot reduce them to the disadvantage of an incumbent judge.
• The post-retirement bar for SC judges is among the strongest globally — intended to prevent influence-peddling.

statement_analysis.statement: After retirement, a Supreme Court judge is prohibited from practising in any court or before any authority in India, whereas a retired High Court judge is prohibited only from practising before the High Court in which he or she served.
statement_analysis.reason: अनुच्छेद 124(7) सेवानिवृत्त सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों को भारत के किसी भी न्यायालय या प्राधिकरण के समक्ष अभ्यास करने से रोकता है। अनुच्छेद 220 सेवानिवृत्त उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों को केवल उस उच्च न्यायालय के समक्ष अभ्यास करने से रोकता है जहाँ वे स्थायी न्यायाधीश थे — वे अन्य उच्च न्यायालयों या सुप्रीम कोर्ट में प्रकट हो सकते हैं।

solution.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प c एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला है क्योंकि जो छात्र सेवानिवृत्ति आयु जानते हैं वे मान सकते हैं कि उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों के लिए सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद की रोक अधिक व्यापक है, जिससे कथन 2 गलत प्रतीत होता है।
elimination_logic: कथन 1 सही है — सुप्रीम कोर्ट के लिए 65 वर्ष (अनुच्छेद 124) और उच्च न्यायालय के लिए 62 वर्ष (अनुच्छेद 217)।
कथन 2 सही है — सुप्रीम कोर्ट के लिए रोक पूर्ण है (अनुच्छेद 124(7)); उच्च न्यायालय के लिए रोक केवल उस विशेष उच्च न्यायालय तक सीमित है (अनुच्छेद 220)।
दोनों कथन सही हैं — विकल्प (a) चुनें।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद की रोक में असमानता ही जाल है। छात्र यह मान लेते हैं कि उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों के लिए रोक सुप्रीम कोर्ट के समान है और सभी न्यायालयों तक फैली हुई है। अनुच्छेद 220 संकीर्ण रूप से लिखा गया है — यह केवल उस विशेष उच्च न्यायालय को रोकता है जहाँ न्यायाधीश स्थायी थे, न कि सभी न्यायालयों को। इससे ऐसा होता है कि एक सेवानिवृत्त उच्च न्यायालय का न्यायाधीश सुप्रीम कोर्ट के समक्ष प्रकट हो सकता है, जो कई छात्रों को असामान्य लगता है।
solution.final_explanation:
सुप्रीम कोर्ट और उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों की सेवा शर्तों और सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद की रोक के लिए दो अलग-अलग संवैधानिक प्रावधान हैं।

• कथन 1 — सही: सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीश 65 वर्ष की आयु में सेवानिवृत्त होते हैं (अनुच्छेद 124(2)); उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश 62 वर्ष में (अनुच्छेद 217(1))। यह तीन वर्ष का अंतर UPSC में एक मानक परीक्षण बिंदु है।
• कथन 2 — सही: अनुच्छेद 124(7) सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों के लिए सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद पूर्ण रोक लगाता है — वे भारत के किसी भी न्यायालय या प्राधिकरण के समक्ष प्रकट नहीं हो सकते। अनुच्छेद 220 केवल उस विशेष उच्च न्यायालय को रोकता है जहाँ वे स्थायी न्यायाधीश थे। एक सेवानिवृत्त उच्च न्यायालय का न्यायाधीश सुप्रीम कोर्ट या अन्य उच्च न्यायालयों के समक्ष प्रकट हो सकता है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों का वेतन भारत के समेकित कोष से दिया जाता है; उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों का वेतन संबंधित राज्य के समेकित कोष से।
• संसद सेवा शर्तों को भविष्य के लिए बदल सकती है लेकिन वर्तमान न्यायाधीश के नुकसान में नहीं कर सकती।
• सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों के लिए सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद की रोक विश्व में सबसे कड़ी में से एक है — इसका उद्देश्य प्रभाव-खरीद को रोकना है।

solution.concept_anchor: Oath of HC judges — administered by Governor
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students associate oath-taking for high constitutional offices with the President, and the CJI administering oaths within the judiciary reinforces that instinct.
elimination_logic: Article 219 governs HC judge oaths — administered by the Governor of the state.
Eliminate President (SC judges' oath authority) and CJI (other SC judges' oath authority).
Select option (c): Governor of the concerned state.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the natural assumption that since the President appoints HC judges, the President or a central authority also administers their oath. Article 219 specifically designates the Governor — consistent with the state-level character of High Courts. Students who conflate the appointment authority with the oath-administering authority fall into this trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The oath of a High Court judge is governed by Article 219, read with the Third Schedule of the Constitution.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The President administers the oath to SC judges under Article 124(6), not HC judges.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Chief Justice of India administers oaths to other SC judges — the President directly administers oath to the CJI.
• Option (c) — Correct: Under Article 219, every HC judge takes the oath before the Governor of the state. The form of oath is prescribed in the Third Schedule.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Chief Justice of the High Court does not administer the oath to newly appointed HC judges.

Value Addition:
• Third Schedule prescribes the exact form — judges swear to 'uphold the Constitution and the laws'.
• The President administers the oath of CJI directly (not through the outgoing CJI).
• For acting HC Chief Justice (Article 223), the Governor appoints — consistent with the Governor's role in HC matters.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: यह भ्रम पैदा करने वाली चाल इस प्राकृतिक धारणा का फायदा उठाती है कि चूंकि राष्ट्रपति उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों की नियुक्ति करते हैं, अतः राष्ट्रपति या कोई केंद्रीय प्राधिकारी उनकी शपथ भी दिलाता होगा। अनुच्छेद 219 स्पष्ट रूप से राज्यपाल को नामित करता है — जो उच्च न्यायालयों के राज्य-स्तरीय स्वरूप के अनुरूप है। जो छात्र नियुक्ति प्राधिकारी को शपथ दिलाने वाले प्राधिकारी के साथ भ्रमित करते हैं, वे इस जाल में फंस जाते हैं।

उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की शपथ अनुच्छेद 219 के साथ संविधान की तीसरी अनुसूची के अनुसार होती है।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: अनुच्छेद 124(6) के तहत राष्ट्रपति सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों को शपथ दिलाते हैं, उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों को नहीं।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश अन्य सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों को शपथ दिलाते हैं — राष्ट्रपति सीधे CJI को शपथ दिलाते हैं।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: अनुच्छेद 219 के तहत प्रत्येक उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश को राज्य के राज्यपाल के समक्ष शपथ लेनी होती है। शपथ का प्रारूप तीसरी अनुसूची में निर्धारित है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: संबंधित उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश नव नियुक्त न्यायाधीशों को शपथ नहीं दिलाते।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• तीसरी अनुसूची में शपथ का सटीक प्रारूप निर्धारित है — न्यायाधीश संविधान और कानूनों का पालन करने की शपथ लेते हैं।
• राष्ट्रपति सीधे CJI को शपथ दिलाते हैं (पूर्व CJI के माध्यम से नहीं)।
• कार्यवाहक उच्च न्यायालय के मुख्य न्यायाधीश (अनुच्छेद 223) के लिए राज्यपाल नियुक्ति करते हैं — जो उच्च न्यायालय मामलों में राज्यपाल की भूमिका के अनुरूप है।

solution.concept_anchor: Collegium — no constitutional basis, judge-made law
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know the 99th Amendment was struck down may conflate 'the collegium was validated by the Amendment' with 'the collegium finds its basis in the Amendment.'
elimination_logic: Judges Inquiry Act governs impeachment investigation, not appointments — eliminate (b).
99th Amendment created NJAC to replace the collegium, not validate it — eliminate (c).
No Judicial Appointments Regulation Act exists — eliminate (d).
Collegium is entirely judge-made through interpretation of Article 124(2) — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap targets students who know the collegium is judge-made but are unsure whether Parliament ever codified it. The Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 sounds procedurally relevant; the 99th Amendment is the most recent and prominent judicial appointment legislation. Both are real laws but neither is the basis of the collegium.
solution.final_explanation:
The collegium system is India's most significant example of judge-made constitutional law — it has no textual foundation in any article or schedule of the Constitution, nor in any statute.

• Option (a): Correct. The collegium was created through judicial interpretation of 'consultation' in Article 124(2) across the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). No constitutional amendment or legislation established it.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 governs only the three-member investigative committee for impeachment proceedings — it has nothing to do with appointments.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) created the NJAC to displace the collegium. When the SC struck it down in 2015, the collegium revived by default — but the Amendment was not its source.
• Option (d): Incorrect. No such legislation exists — a fabricated option.

Value Addition:
• Since the collegium is judge-made, Parliament cannot amend it directly — it would require a constitutional amendment or another Presidential Reference.
• The Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) governs the operational mechanics of collegium recommendations but also lacks constitutional status.
• The collegium's opacity is the primary criticism — it operates without statutory transparency requirements.

solution.concept_anchor: HC judge eligibility — no distinguished jurist, no minimum age

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution prescribes a minimum age for appointment as a High Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(2) does not prescribe any minimum age for HC judges — this is commonly assumed but is not a constitutional requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: A person who has been an advocate of a High Court for ten years is eligible to be appointed as a High Court judge.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 217(2)(b) provides that a person who has been an advocate of one or more High Courts for ten years is eligible for appointment as HC judge.

statement_analysis.statement: The eligibility criterion of 'distinguished jurist' is available for appointment to both the Supreme Court and the High Court under their respective constitutional provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(3)(c) provides the distinguished jurist route only for SC appointments. Article 217(2) for HC judges contains no such category.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who vaguely recall that distinguished jurists can be appointed to courts and assume this applies to HCs as well.
elimination_logic: No minimum age in Article 217(2) — Statement 1 incorrect.
10-year HC advocacy qualifies under Article 217(2)(b) — Statement 2 correct.
Distinguished jurist category absent from Article 217(2) — Statement 3 incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate: (1) Students assume minimum age is prescribed because many countries and even some Indian statutes use age thresholds. (2) The distinguished jurist category sounds prestigious and is assumed to apply to both courts. Article 217(2) is silent on both — and that silence is the constitutional rule.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 217(2) defines HC judge eligibility with precision, and what it omits is as important as what it includes.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: No minimum age is prescribed in Article 217(2). Unlike the US (which has no minimum age either, but informally) or some state frameworks, India's constitutional text is silent on age for both SC and HC judges.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 217(2)(b) qualifies a person who has been an advocate of one or more HCs for at least 10 years. This is one of two qualifying routes for HC judges.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The distinguished jurist category appears only in Article 124(3)(c) for SC appointments. It has never been used even for SC, and it has no equivalent in HC eligibility under Article 217(2).

Value Addition:
• HC judge can also qualify by holding a judicial office in India for 10 years — Article 217(2)(a).
• Both HC eligibility routes require Indian citizenship.
• SC eligibility has a third route (HC judge for 5 years) with a shorter tenure requirement than the HC advocacy route.

अनुच्छेद 217(2) उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश की पात्रता को स्पष्ट रूप से परिभाषित करता है, और जो इसमें नहीं है वह उतना ही महत्वपूर्ण है जितना कि जो इसमें है।

• कथन 1 — गलत: अनुच्छेद 217(2) में कोई न्यूनतम आयु निर्धारित नहीं है। अमेरिका की तरह (जहाँ औपचारिक रूप से कोई न्यूनतम आयु नहीं है, लेकिन अनौपचारिक रूप से है) या कुछ राज्य के ढांचे की तरह, भारत के संवैधानिक पाठ में उच्च न्यायालय और सर्वोच्च न्यायालय दोनों के लिए आयु पर मौन है।
• कथन 2 — सही: अनुच्छेद 217(2)(b) के अनुसार, जो व्यक्ति एक या अधिक उच्च न्यायालयों का कम से कम 10 वर्षों तक अधिवक्ता रहा हो, वह पात्र है। यह उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश बनने के दो मार्गों में से एक है।
• कथन 3 — गलत: प्रतिष्ठित न्यायविद की श्रेणी केवल अनुच्छेद 124(3)(c) में सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की नियुक्ति के लिए है। इसे सर्वोच्च न्यायालय के लिए भी कभी उपयोग नहीं किया गया है, और अनुच्छेद 217(2) के तहत उच्च न्यायालय की पात्रता में इसका कोई समकक्ष नहीं है।

• दोनों उच्च न्यायालय पात्रता मार्गों के लिए भारतीय नागरिकता आवश्यक है।
• सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की पात्रता का तीसरा मार्ग है (5 वर्षों तक उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीश रहना), जो उच्च न्यायालय के अधिवक्ता मार्ग की तुलना में कम अवधि की आवश्यकता रखता है।

solution.concept_anchor: Article 224A — retired HC judge consent requirement

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 224, the President may appoint additional judges to a High Court for a period not exceeding two years to deal with a temporary increase in the business of the Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 224(1) explicitly allows the President to appoint additional judges for up to two years to address temporary increases in business or arrears — this statement is factually accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 224A, the appointment of a retired High Court judge to sit and act in a High Court requires only the consent of the President — the retired judge's personal consent is not needed.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 224A requires the consent of both the retired judge AND the President. The retired judge's personal consent is expressly required — the initiating request is made by the Chief Justice of the HC, but the judge cannot be compelled.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 223 empowers the Governor (not the President) to appoint an acting Chief Justice of a High Court when the office of the Chief Justice is vacant.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 223 provides that the Governor shall appoint a judge of the High Court to perform the duties of Chief Justice when the office is vacant or the incumbent is absent — this is correctly stated.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (3 only) is a strong distractor because Statement 3 is correct (and therefore not a 'NOT correct' answer), and students who quickly confirm Statement 3 may stop there.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct as per Article 224(1) — not the answer.
Statement 2 incorrectly omits the retired judge's mandatory personal consent — this is NOT correct.
Statement 3 correctly identifies the Governor under Article 223 — not the answer.
Select option (b): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 replaces the retired judge's mandatory consent with only the President's consent. Students who recall 'President is involved in 224A' stop at that and mark it correct. The critical additional requirement — that the retired judge personally must agree — is what many students miss. This mirrors the distinction between Articles 127 and 128 regarding HC vs SC judges.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 223 and 224 deal with temporary and acting judicial appointments at the High Court level, each with distinct procedural requirements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 224(1) empowers the President to appoint additional HC judges for up to two years to meet temporary increases in business or arrears. Not a 'NOT correct' statement.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: Article 224A requires both the consent of the President AND the personal consent of the retired HC judge. The provision is initiated by the HC Chief Justice's request — but the retired judge cannot be compelled. Omitting the retired judge's consent makes this statement incorrect.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 223 assigns the Governor (not the President) the role of appointing an acting Chief Justice of a HC when the office is vacant or the incumbent is absent. Not a 'NOT correct' statement.

Value Addition:
• Under Article 224A, the initiating authority is the Chief Justice of the HC, not the President or Governor.
• Additional judges under Article 224 cannot be appointed beyond 2 years — they must either be confirmed as permanent judges or their additional tenure ends.
• The Governor's role in Article 223 contrasts with the President's role in Article 126 for acting CJI.

solution.concept_anchor: MoP — no constitutional or statutory basis

statement_analysis.statement: The Memorandum of Procedure governing the collegium's recommendations has been given statutory backing through an amendment to the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968.
statement_analysis.reason: The MoP has no statutory or constitutional backing — it is an administrative arrangement between the executive and the judiciary. No amendment to the Judges Inquiry Act has formalised it.

statement_analysis.statement: If the Government returns a collegium recommendation and the collegium reiterates it, the Government is constitutionally bound to accept the reiterated recommendation.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Second Judges Case (1993), the reiteration rule has been established — the government may return a recommendation once, but if the collegium reiterates it, acceptance is constitutionally mandated.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know the reiteration rule may assume both statements are correct without checking the MoP's legal status.
elimination_logic: MoP has no statutory basis — Judges Inquiry Act does not cover it. Statement 1 incorrect.
Reiteration rule from 1993 jurisprudence — government must accept reaffirmed collegium recommendation. Statement 2 correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication in Statement 1 targets students who know the MoP is administratively important and assume it must have some legislative basis — particularly given post-NJAC controversy. The Judges Inquiry Act sounds relevant to judicial governance, creating a compelling false association. The MoP's lack of any legal foundation is precisely its weakness in the executive-judiciary standoff.
solution.final_explanation:
The Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) occupies a peculiar constitutional space — it is operationally central to judicial appointments but legally peripheral.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The MoP is purely an administrative arrangement developed between the government and the Supreme Court. It has no statutory basis, no constitutional provision, and has not been incorporated into the Judges Inquiry Act or any other legislation. This administrative character is also its weakness — the government can delay implementing it.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Established through the Second Judges Case (1993) and reinforced by the Third Judges Case (1998) — if the collegium reiterates a recommendation, the government loses its discretion to withhold. However, critics note that the government has used delay (a 'pocket veto') to circumvent this in practice.

Value Addition:
• MoP renegotiations have been ongoing since 2016 (post-NJAC) without conclusion.
• The government's primary tool is delay — it cannot formally reject a reiterated recommendation but can sit on it indefinitely.
• RTI applicability to CJI's office (2019 SC judgment) increased transparency pressure on the collegium.

• कथन 1 — गलत: MoP पूरी तरह से सरकार और सुप्रीम कोर्ट के बीच विकसित एक प्रशासनिक व्यवस्था है। इसका कोई वैधानिक आधार, कोई संवैधानिक प्रावधान नहीं है, और न ही इसे जजेस इन्क्वायरी एक्ट या किसी अन्य कानून में शामिल किया गया है। यह प्रशासनिक स्वरूप इसकी कमजोरी भी है — सरकार इसे लागू करने में देरी कर सकती है।
• कथन 2 — सही: द्वितीय जज केस (1993) और तृतीय जज केस (1998) के माध्यम से स्थापित — यदि कोलेजियम सिफारिश को पुनः दोहराता है, तो सरकार के पास उसे अस्वीकार करने की छूट नहीं रहती। हालांकि आलोचक कहते हैं कि सरकार ने व्यवहार में देरी ('पॉकेट वीटो') का उपयोग किया है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• MoP के पुनर्विचार 2016 से (NJAC के बाद) जारी हैं लेकिन निष्कर्ष नहीं निकला।
• सरकार का मुख्य उपकरण देरी है — वह पुनः दोहराई गई सिफारिश को औपचारिक रूप से अस्वीकार नहीं कर सकती लेकिन उसे अनिश्चितकाल तक टाल सकती है।
• CJI के कार्यालय पर RTI लागू होने (2019 SC निर्णय) से कोलेजियम पर पारदर्शिता का दबाव बढ़ा।

The constitutional framework for judicial appointments contains no diversity mandate, making this a case where the Constitution's silence is the operative rule.

• Option (a): Incorrect. No constitutional provision mandates reservation or minimum representation for any community, gender, or social group in judicial appointments. Article 124 sets only eligibility criteria.

• India has not yet had a woman Chief Justice of India.
• Constitutional silence on diversity in judiciary contrasts with Article 16(4)'s reservation provisions for state employment.

statement_analysis.statement: From 2017 onwards, the Supreme Court collegium began publishing reasons for its recommendations and transfers on the Supreme Court's official website.
statement_analysis.reason: The collegium started publishing reasons for recommendations and transfers in 2017 as a self-initiated transparency measure — a landmark development in collegium accountability.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court held in 2019 that the Chief Justice of India's office is a 'public authority' under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
statement_analysis.reason: In 2019, the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench held that the CJI's office falls within the definition of 'public authority' under the RTI Act, making it subject to information disclosure obligations.

statement_analysis.statement: Publishing reasons for collegium recommendations is a constitutional mandate introduced through an amendment to Article 124.
statement_analysis.reason: Publishing reasons is a collegium's own self-imposed practice — it has no constitutional or statutory mandate and is not the result of any amendment to Article 124.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know statements 1 and 2 are correct and assume the constitutional-mandate framing in Statement 3 must also be true given recent judicial reform discourse.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correct — 2017 transparency initiative by collegium.
Statement 2 correct — 2019 RTI judgment on CJI's office.
Statement 3 incorrect — no constitutional amendment mandates publication of reasons.
Select option (c): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the scope-extension trap by attributing constitutional status to what is only an administrative self-regulation. Students who are aware of recent transparency steps may not stop to verify whether they were constitutionally mandated or merely voluntary. The absence of any Article 124 amendment is the decisive fact.
solution.final_explanation:
Recent developments in collegium transparency represent a significant but legally informal shift in how judicial appointments are governed.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Since 2017, the collegium has published its reasons for recommendations and transfers on the SC website. This was a response to criticism of opacity and was initiated by the collegium itself.
• Statement 2 — Correct: In Chief Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), a five-judge Constitution Bench held that the CJI's office is a 'public authority' under the RTI Act.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No constitutional amendment touches on the publication of collegium reasons. Article 124 has not been amended for this purpose. The transparency initiative is self-imposed — the collegium can reverse it without any parliamentary or constitutional process.

Value Addition:
• RTI applicability to CJI's office does not override judicial privilege in individual case materials.
• Publishing reasons creates a de facto accountability record but lacks enforceability.
• The tension between judicial privacy in personal matters and public accountability in appointments is an ethics paper theme.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here involves extending the collegium's constitutional mandate (which is specific to SC and HC) to cover tribunals. The SC's intervention in tribunal appointments is real and ongoing, but its concern has been executive overreach, not the absence of collegium. Students who conflate 'judicial independence' with 'collegium mechanism' will wrongly pick option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Tribunal appointments represent a contested zone at the intersection of executive authority, parliamentary legislation, and judicial independence doctrine.

Assertion Analysis: Factually accurate. Tribunal members are appointed through search-cum-selection committees constituted under statute — not through the SC collegium. This is a structural distinction between constitutional courts (SC, HC) and statutory tribunals.

Reason Analysis: Correct. The Supreme Court in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2021) struck down several provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 — particularly those reducing the tenure of members and altering the search committee's composition in ways that gave the executive disproportionate control.

Causal Relationship: R does not explain A. The reason the collegium is absent from tribunal appointments is not the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 (which is recent). The collegium was always limited to constitutional courts. The SC's objection to the 2021 Act was about executive dominance in tribunal management, not the absence of collegium participation.

Value Addition:
• The Rojer Mathew case (2019) also addressed tribunal appointments and referred to a five-judge bench.
• Tribunals function under the executive domain but their adjudicatory independence is protected under Article 14.
• Parliamentary control over tribunal service conditions is permissible but cannot compromise adjudicatory independence.

solution.concept_anchor: Impeachment — same session requirement and dual majority

statement_analysis.statement: Both Houses of Parliament must pass the impeachment address in the same session.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution requires that both Houses pass the address in the same session — if the session lapses after one House passes it, the process must restart.

statement_analysis.statement: The special majority required for impeachment — majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting — must be satisfied in each House independently.
statement_analysis.reason: Both conditions (absolute majority + 2/3 qualified majority) must be met in each House separately, not jointly across Houses.

statement_analysis.statement: The impeachment address can be initiated only in the Rajya Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The impeachment address can be initiated in either House of Parliament — there is no constitutional requirement that it begin in a specific House.

statement_analysis.statement: Upon presentation of an impeachment address by Parliament, the President is bound to remove the judge — the President has no discretion.
statement_analysis.reason: Once Parliament passes the address under Article 124(4), the President must issue the order of removal — the President retains no discretion at this stage.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two) is a strong distractor because students who identify Statement 3 as incorrect may also doubt Statement 4, assuming the President retains some discretion even after Parliament's address.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correct — same session requirement confirmed.
Statement 2 correct — dual majority per House.
Statement 3 incorrect — either House can originate the address.
Statement 4 correct — President has no post-address discretion.
Three correct statements — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the common student assumption that impeachment begins in the Rajya Sabha (because the Justice V. Ramaswami motion famously originated there). In constitutional text, no such restriction exists — the address can originate in either House. Statement 4 is the second trap: students who associate Presidential discretion broadly may assume the President can withhold the removal order, but Article 124(4) leaves no discretion post-address.
solution.final_explanation:
The impeachment process for SC judges under Article 124(4) has several procedural nuances that are commonly misunderstood.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Both Houses must act in same session | Correct |
| Dual majority met independently in each House | Correct |
| Address can only be initiated in Rajya Sabha | Incorrect |
| President has no discretion post-address | Correct |

Three of four statements are correct.

Value Addition:
• The Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 investigation precedes the address — the three-member committee must conclude its inquiry first.
• Grounds for removal: only proved misbehaviour or incapacity — both must be 'proved', not merely alleged.
• The same process applies to HC judges via Article 218, to the CAG under Article 148, and (post-2023) to Election Commissioners.

• Option (a): Incorrect. India's collegium is a judge-only body with no independent commission structure or civil society representation.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The US uses Presidential nomination followed by Senate confirmation — a political process involving the executive and legislature, not an independent commission.

• JAC's recommendations go to the Lord Chancellor (executive), who has limited power to reject.

solution.concept_anchor: In-House Procedure — no statutory basis, judge can refuse to resign
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know the In-House Procedure exists assume it carries legal enforceability, making option (a) seem like a valid intermediate step before formal impeachment.
elimination_logic: In-House Procedure has no legal enforceability — cannot compel resignation. Eliminate (a).
No collective SC judge mechanism can remove a judge — eliminate (b).
Transfer under Article 222 is for HC judges — eliminate (d).
Article 124(4) parliamentary address is the only valid path — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication in option (b) targets students who conflate institutional authority with legal authority — a collective decision by SC judges sounds authoritative but has no constitutional backing. Option (a)'s In-House Procedure is real but non-enforceable, creating the illusion of a legal intermediate step. Recognising that no mechanism short of Article 124(4) can remove an SC judge is the key insight.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional protection of SC judges is designed to be robust — only one mechanism can result in their removal, and it requires Parliament.

Applicable principle: Article 124(4) provides the sole path for removal of an SC judge — a parliamentary address with dual special majority in both Houses in the same session. The In-House Procedure is a self-regulatory tool but has no legal teeth.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The In-House Procedure can request voluntary resignation and the CJI may withdraw the judge from judicial work, but it cannot compel removal. The judge retains the legal right to refuse.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: No constitutional mechanism allows a majority of sitting SC judges to remove a colleague — collective judicial opinion has no removal authority outside the collegium's appointment role.
• Option (c) — Correct: The only constitutionally valid path is the parliamentary impeachment process under Article 124(4), initiated by a notice of motion signed by at least 100 members of Lok Sabha or 50 members of Rajya Sabha.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Transfer under Article 222 applies to HC judges, not SC judges, and is not a disciplinary removal mechanism.

Value Addition:
• The 100/50 member threshold for notice is from the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968, not the Constitution directly.
• CJI can withdraw cases from an accused judge pending investigation — a non-statutory interim measure.
• The In-House Procedure's legitimacy rests entirely on judicial culture, not legal authority.

लागू सिद्धांत: अनुच्छेद 124(4) सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीश को हटाने का एकमात्र मार्ग प्रदान करता है — दोनों सदनों में उसी सत्र में द्वि-विशेष बहुमत के साथ संसदीय प्रस्ताव। इन-हाउस प्रक्रिया एक स्व-नियामक उपकरण है लेकिन इसका कोई कानूनी दांत नहीं है।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: इन-हाउस प्रक्रिया स्वैच्छिक इस्तीफा मांग सकती है और CJI न्यायाधीश को न्यायिक कार्य से हटा सकता है, लेकिन हटाने के लिए बाध्य नहीं कर सकता। न्यायाधीश के पास मना करने का कानूनी अधिकार है।

• विकल्प (c) — सही: संवैधानिक रूप से वैध एकमात्र मार्ग अनुच्छेद 124(4) के तहत संसदीय महाभियोग प्रक्रिया है, जिसे कम से कम 100 लोकसभा सदस्यों या 50 राज्यसभा सदस्यों के हस्ताक्षरित प्रस्ताव द्वारा शुरू किया जाता है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: अनुच्छेद 222 के तहत स्थानांतरण उच्च न्यायालय के न्यायाधीशों के लिए है, सुप्रीम कोर्ट के न्यायाधीशों के लिए नहीं, और यह कोई अनुशासनात्मक हटाने की प्रक्रिया नहीं है।

• CJI जांच के दौरान आरोपी न्यायाधीश से मामले वापस ले सकता है — एक गैर-कानूनी अंतरिम उपाय।

Students who know the Governor is a consultee for HC appointments reflexively apply it to transfers — a classic conflation of two related but distinct processes that both involve HC judges and the President.
solution.final_explanation:
The consultation architecture differs across four judicial appointment/transfer scenarios — getting the matchings right requires precisely distinguishing each.

Correct pairings:
• A (HC judge appointment — Article 217) — 2: Three mandatory consultees: CJI, Governor of the state, Chief Justice of that HC. All three required.
• B (HC judge transfer — Article 222) — 4: Only the CJI's opinion is required; Governor's concurrence and the judge's consent are not needed. Post-1993, CJI collegium's opinion is binding.
• C (SC judge appointment — Article 124(2)) — 1: CJI is mandatory; other SC and HC judges consulted as President deems necessary. Governor is never a consultee.
• D (Collegium for HC appointments) — 3: The collegium for HC appointments consists of CJI plus 2 senior-most SC judges — smaller than the 5-member SC appointment collegium.

The trap pairing is B (transfer) and A (appointment) — both involve HC judges and Presidential action, but their consultee lists are entirely different.

Value Addition:
• HC appointment collegium (CJI + 2) vs. SC appointment collegium (CJI + 4) — size distinction is frequently tested.
• Post-Second Judges Case, 'consultation' in both Articles 217 and 222 became 'concurrence' in practice.
• Governor's role in HC matters is more extensive than in SC matters — a constitutional design reflecting HCs' state character.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because the CAG is a central-level constitutional officer, and students assume his salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India like SC judges — but this is actually correct, making (b) NOT the odd one out.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap presents HC judges alongside SC judges and the CAG — all constitutional officers whose salaries are non-votable. solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the distinction between central and state Consolidated Funds in the context of judicial financial independence.

• Option (a) — Belongs: SC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 146(3) — non-votable, ensuring independence from parliamentary budgetary control.
• Option (b) — Belongs: The CAG's salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 148(6) — same mechanism as SC judges.
• Option (c) — Does NOT belong: HC judges' salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the concerned State, not the Consolidated Fund of India. Article 229(3) governs this. The state-level character of HCs is reflected in their financial arrangement.
• Option (d) — Belongs: Attorney General of India's remuneration is determined by the President and paid from the Consolidated Fund of India.

Value Addition:
• 'Charged to Consolidated Fund' means the amount is not subject to vote in the legislature — a constitutional guarantee of financial autonomy.
• Parliament can change HC judge salaries (since they come from State funds via central legislation) — an indirect lever.
• After the 7th Pay Commission, administrative expenses of HCs are partly met by the Centre.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chief Justice of India administers the oath to all other judges of the Supreme Court, including the oath of the next incoming Chief Justice.
statement_analysis.reason: The CJI administers the oath to other SC judges. However, the President of India administers the oath to the Chief Justice of India directly — the outgoing or sitting CJI does not swear in the next CJI.

statement_analysis.statement: The form of oath taken by judges of both the Supreme Court and the High Court requires them to 'uphold the Constitution and the laws' — not merely to 'bear true faith and allegiance' to the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Third Schedule forms of oath for judges include both allegiance to the Constitution AND the specific duty to 'uphold the Constitution and the laws' — this is correctly stated and therefore NOT a 'not correct' answer.

statement_analysis.statement: Since the Chief Justice of India is appointed by the President, it follows constitutionally that the President must administer the oath to all judges of the Supreme Court, including those appointed on the CJI's recommendation.
statement_analysis.reason: The President administers the oath only to the CJI. For other SC judges, it is the CJI who administers the oath under the practice derived from Article 124(6) and the Third Schedule — not the President for each individual judge.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (2 only) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is the correct one, leading students to think it is the 'not correct' answer in the absence of careful reading.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is NOT correct — President swears in CJI, not outgoing CJI.
Statement 2 is correct — judges do swear to uphold the Constitution and laws.
Statement 3 is NOT correct — President swears in only CJI, not all SC judges.
Select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets who administers the oath to whom. Students readily recall 'President administers oath to CJI' but often extend this to all SC judges — or conversely, assume the outgoing CJI swears in the next CJI. Both errors are triggered by different students, and both lead to wrong answers on statements about the oath administration chain.
solution.final_explanation:
The oath administration chain for SC judges is precise and worth memorising exactly.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: The CJI administers the oath to other SC judges. But the CJI's own oath is administered by the President of India — not the outgoing CJI. Statement 1 is incorrect in claiming the CJI swears in the next CJI.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Third Schedule form for judges requires them to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution AND to uphold the Constitution and the laws. This dual formulation distinguishes the judicial oath from the parliamentary oath (which emphasises allegiance). Not a 'not correct' answer.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The President administers the oath only to the CJI, not to all SC judges. For all other SC judges, the CJI administers the oath. This is a clear entity-swap error in Statement 3.

Value Addition:
• HC judges take their oath before the Governor — not the President or CJI.
• Third Schedule prescribes the verbatim form of all constitutional oaths.
• Solemn affirmation is an alternative to oath — available under the same Third Schedule provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because it correctly orders the first three events but places the Presidential Reference (1998) before the NJAC case (2015) — a plausible ordering that students may accept without noticing that option (a) has the same ordering.
elimination_logic: First Judges Case: 1981 — must come first.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates between the Third Judges Case (1998) and the NJAC case (2015). While most students know both events, placing the Presidential Reference precisely in 1998 and the NJAC case in 2015 requires accurate recall. Option (c) is designed to look identical to (a) at a glance — only careful reading reveals they present the same sequence, with option (b) and (d) containing the actual wrong orderings.
solution.final_explanation:
The Four Judges Cases span 34 years and represent the complete arc of judicial appointment jurisprudence in India.

Correct sequence:
1. First Judges Case — S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981): Seven-judge bench upheld executive primacy; CJI's opinion advisory.
2. Second Judges Case — SCARA v. Union of India (1993): Nine-judge bench reversed 1981 ruling; 'consultation' = 'concurrence'; collegium of CJI + 2 senior judges.
3. Third Judges Case — Presidential Reference (1998): Ten-judge bench; collegium expanded to CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges; definition of 'consultation' clarified.
4. Fourth Judges Case / NJAC Case — Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015): Five-judge bench (4:1) struck down the 99th Amendment and NJAC.

Wrong options fail by reversing 1993 and 1998, or by placing the NJAC case before 1998.

Value Addition:
• The 2015 judgment is sometimes called the 'Fourth Judges Case' — important for examination identification.
• Each case involved increasingly larger benches: 7, 9, 10, and 5 judges.
• The 1998 Presidential Reference is unique — the only instance of the executive seeking clarification from SC on judicial appointments.

solution.concept_anchor: CJI appointment — convention not constitutional mandate for seniority

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution of India explicitly mandates that the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court must be appointed as the Chief Justice of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(2) gives the President discretion in appointing the CJI — seniority is a constitutional convention, not a textual or legal requirement in the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: The conventions of seniority governing the appointment of the Chief Justice of India were violated on two occasions — in 1973 and 1977 — when senior judges were superseded in favour of candidates preferred by the executive.
statement_analysis.reason: In 1973, Justice A.N. Ray was appointed CJI superseding three senior judges; in 1977, Justice M.H. Beg was appointed superseding Justice H.R. Khanna — both are historically documented supersessions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know the seniority convention is strongly established may conflate 'well-established convention' with 'constitutional mandate', leading them to mark Statement 1 as correct.
elimination_logic: Article 124(2) has no seniority text — Statement 1 is incorrect.
1973 and 1977 supersessions are historically verified — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 converts a powerful convention into a constitutional mandate by adding the word 'explicitly mandates.' Students who know seniority governs CJI appointment in practice may not stop to verify whether the Constitution actually says so. It does not — and this distinction between convention and constitutional text is a classic UPSC precision test.
solution.final_explanation:
The appointment of the Chief Justice of India illustrates the gap between constitutional text and constitutional practice.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 124(2) grants the President discretion to appoint the CJI after consultation — it says nothing about seniority. The seniority norm is an unwritten constitutional convention that evolved to protect judicial independence, not a legal requirement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The supersession of 1973 (Justice A.N. Ray appointed over three senior judges — Shelat, Hegde, Grover) and 1977 (Justice M.H. Beg appointed superseding Justice H.R. Khanna, who had dissented in ADM Jabalpur) are historically documented violations of the seniority convention.

Value Addition:
• Post-1977, the seniority convention has been consistently followed — no supersession has occurred since.
• Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur (habeas corpus case during Emergency) is widely regarded as an act of judicial courage.
• The seniority convention is so entrenched post-1993 that it now functions as a near-binding norm, even without constitutional text.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know HC appointments involve more consultees than SC appointments may incorrectly extend this to the removal procedure, assuming HC removal must also be more complex.
